1.title: Meg Picks a Pet
1.topic: Meg wants a pet and looks at a napping cat, a pecking hen and a digging pig before a pup hops up on her lap and she picks it (pets, animals, choices, feelings)
lines: Will Meg *pick* the *cat*? ↗ | The *cat* *naps* and *naps*. | *Not* *that* one. ↘
Will Meg *pick* the *hen*? ↗ | The *hen* *pecks* and *pecks*. | *Not* *that* one. ↘
Will Meg *pick* the *pig*? ↗ | The *pig* *digs* and *digs*. | *Not* *that* one. ↘
Will Meg *pick* the *pup*? ↗ | The *pup* *hops* up on her *lap*! ↘
sounds: 짧고 가볍게 '이': pick '픽', pig '피그'. '피-익'처럼 길게 늘이지 않아요.
입을 살짝 벌리고 짧게 '에': pet '펫', hen '헨'.
ck는 'k' 소리 하나예요: pick '픽', lick '릭'. 끝에 '으'를 붙이지 않아요.
1.expression: Ask each “Will Meg pick the …?” with a rising, curious voice, read the animal actions with a steady beat, shake your head on “Not that one,” sound surprised when the pup hops up, and end with a big happy “Yes! This one!”
practice: The pup hops up on her lap!

2.title: Six Points on My Mitten
2.topic: on the first snowy morning a girl catches snowflakes on her dark blue mitten, notices their six points and that each one looks different, then rushes inside to show Mom but they melt (seasons, weather, science, family)
lines: Lily *rushed* *inside* to *show* *Mom*, | but the snowflakes had *melted*. ↘
sounds: t·d 소리 뒤에서만 '이드'가 한 박자 더 생겨요: landed '랜디드', melted '멜티드'.
k·s·sh·f 소리 뒤 -ed는 짧은 't': looked '룩트', rushed '러쉬트', laughed '래프트'.
가볍게 'd'만 붙여요: pulled '풀드', smiled '스마일드'. 한 박자로 읽어요.
2.expression: Sound excited on “It was snowing!”, slow down and look closely on “Lily looked closely,” shout “It has six points!” with wonder, let Lily's question to Dad rise, give Dad a calm, gentle voice, sound a little disappointed on “had melted,” and end with a cheerful laugh.
practice: No two are exactly the same.

3.title: The Yellow Kindness Rock
3.topic: a girl paints a smooth creek rock with a smiling sun and a kind message, hides it under a park bench, sees a lonely older man find it and smile, keeps her secret and paints another one (kindness, community, art, feelings)
lines: The *next* *day*, | she *hid* the rock | under a *bench* at the *park*. ↘
On *Saturday*, | she *saw* an *older* *man* | *sitting* *alone* on the bench. ↘
This *time*, | she *painted* a *red* *heart* | and the words “*Keep* *smiling*!” ↘
sounds: 혀끝을 윗니와 아랫니 사이에 살짝 내밀고 목을 울려요: smooth '스무ð', this. 'ㄷ'나 'ㅈ'로 바꾸지 않아요.
입꼬리를 옆으로 당기고 길게 '이-': creek '크리-크', week '위-크'. 짧은 i (sitting, hid)와 구분해요.
-ing의 ng는 입을 다물지 않고 코로 울려요: smiling '스마일링'. '스마일링그'처럼 끝에 '그'를 붙이지 않아요.
3.expression: Begin in a warm, quiet storyteller voice, read “You are awesome!” brightly as the message, sound curious and a little impatient on “Ava wondered all week,” soften your voice for the older man sitting alone, give him a slow, grateful voice for “It made my whole day,” whisper a little on “she kept her secret,” and end happily on “Keep smiling!”

4.title: The Monarchs' Long Journey
4.topic: monarch butterfly migration: monarchs fly up to about 3,000 miles from Canada and the United States to fir forests in the mountains of Mexico, glide on rising air, sip nectar, use the sun like a compass, cluster on trees all winter, and take three or four generations to return north on milkweed (animals, insects, seasons, science)
lines: They are *monarch* butterflies, | and *many* of them *fly* from *Canada* and the *United* *States* | *all* the way to *Mexico*. ↘
*How* can an *insect* that *weighs* *less* than a *paper* *clip* | fly *that* *far*? ↘
*Scientists* *think* they use the *sun* | like a *compass* | to *find* their way *south*. ↘
So many butterflies *cluster* on the *branches* | that the *trees* *look* *orange*! ↘
It *takes* *three* or *four* *generations* | to get *all* the way *back* *north*. ↘
vocab: 활공하는 것 (날갯짓 없이 미끄러지듯 나는 것)
sounds: 강세 없는 모음은 힘을 빼고 짧은 '어'로: EN-er-gy, COM-pass, gen-er-A-tions처럼 대문자 음절만 세게 읽어요.
자음 사이에 '으'를 넣지 않아요: insect '인섹트'(한 번에), forests '포리스츠', cluster '클러스터r'.
'아이'로 미끄러지듯: fly '플라이', find '파인드'. 짧은 i (sip, milkweed)와 구분해요.
4.expression: Read like an excited nature-show host: sound amazed on “nearly three thousand miles!”, ask “How can an insect … fly that far?” as a real question, explain the gliding and compass lines clearly with a small pause at each /, slow down and picture the scene on “the trees look orange!”, lean in on “Here is the most surprising part,” and end in a hushed, wondering voice on “Nobody knows exactly how they do it!”
